levels.title: First sounds
levels.subtitle: Open strings, your first chord and your first change.

lessons.title: Meet the six strings
theory: Strings are numbered from the thinnest (1st, high E) to the thickest (6th, low E).
Open, from low to high: E – A – D – G – B – E.
Tune before every session: an out-of-tune guitar makes even good playing sound wrong.
tips: Rest the pick on the string and let it go: a firm attack without brushing the neighbors.
If an open string buzzes, check the tuning and make sure your other hand isn't touching it.
tutorials: how to tune a guitar for beginners

exercises.title: Play the 6 open strings, from the 6th to the 1st
And back, from the 1st to the 6th

lessons.title: Parts of the guitar and reading tab
theory: The headstock holds the tuners, the neck holds the frets, and the body holds the bridge (and, on an electric, the pickups).
Frets are counted from the nut: fret 1 is the one closest to the headstock. In tab, 0 means the open string.
Tab draws the six strings as lines with the thinnest (1st string, high E) on top. A number on a line tells you which fret to press.
Read tab from left to right, like text. Numbers stacked in the same column are played together.
tips: Say the string and the fret out loud before you play each number: it makes reading automatic sooner.
tutorials: how to read guitar tab for beginners

lessons.title: Your first chord: E minor
theory: A chord is several notes at once. Em uses only two fingers and all six strings ring.
Middle finger on fret 2 of the 5th string, ring finger on fret 2 of the 4th string.
Press with the fingertip, right behind the metal fret, with the thumb behind the neck.
tips: If a string sounds muted, a finger is touching it: arch your knuckles more.

lessons.title: Am and your first change
theory: Am has the same shape as E, one string lower. Don't play the 6th string.
In the Em→Am change, the middle and ring fingers travel together one string toward the floor.
tips: Practice the change slowly without strumming: look at the shape, then close your eyes.
tutorials: e minor to a minor chord change guitar

levels.title: Open chords
levels.subtitle: The chords behind thousands of songs.

lessons.title: D, A and E
theory: A and E are the same shape moved one string: three fingers (A) versus two plus one (E).
Strum D from the 4th string: the two low strings stay silent.
tutorials: d a e chords guitar beginner

lessons.title: G and C
theory: G uses all six strings; C leaves the 6th out.
With G, C, D and Em you can already play pop's favorite progression: I–V–vi–IV.
tutorials: I V vi IV progression guitar

levels.title: Rhythm
levels.subtitle: Strumming, time signatures and the right hand.

lessons.title: Down and up
theory: The strumming hand swings like a pendulum, always in time, even when it misses the strings.
Down strums land on the numbers (1, 2, 3, 4) and up strums on the "ands".
The pattern D.DU.UDU is counted: 1, 2 and, and 4 and.
tutorials: basic strumming pattern guitar down up

exercises.title: Ballad in C with the metronome

lessons.title: Three-four time
theory: In 3/4 you count ONE-two-three: the first beat is heavier.
E7 is E without the ring finger: the tension that resolves back to Am.

levels.title: Reading rhythm
levels.subtitle: Note values, rests and the pulse, tapped and then played.

lessons.title: The pulse
theory: The pulse is the steady beat you tap with your foot. BPM says how many beats fit in a minute: 60 BPM is one per second.
Most music counts in groups of four (4/4 time). The first beat of each group is the strongest, and the metronome marks it with a higher click.
tips: Tap Space (or the pad) with each note. The first bar is only the count-in: listen before you play.
tutorials: how to count beats in music
captions: Four quarter notes: one note on every beat.

lessons.title: What each note is worth
theory: Each note value says how long the note lasts. In 4/4 the quarter note is one beat, and the others are doubles and halves of it.
Whole note = 4 beats, half note = 2, quarter = 1, eighth = ½, sixteenth = ¼. Every value has a rest that lasts just as long.
tips: In tab, these same values often show up as stems under the fret numbers. Look for them next time you open a song.
tutorials: note values explained whole half quarter eighth

lessons.title: Long notes
theory: With long notes you play once and keep counting while the note rings. The hard part is not rushing the next one.
captions: Two half notes: play on 1 and on 3.

lessons.title: Eighth notes
theory: Eighth notes split each beat in two. Count "one-and, two-and": the note on the "and" falls right between two clicks.
tips: A lot of rock rhythm guitar is steady eighths. Get them even and half the songs get easier.

levels.title: Color
levels.subtitle: Sevenths, blues and power chords.

lessons.title: Sevenths and the blues
theory: A seventh chord adds a note that wants to resolve: that's why the blues always feels in motion.
The 12-bar blues: I I I I · IV IV I I · V IV I V.

lessons.title: Power chords
theory: A power chord is root plus fifth: neither major nor minor, which is why it sounds great with distortion.
It's a movable shape: the same fingering on any fret.

levels.title: Barre chords and melody
levels.subtitle: F with a barre and your first scale.

lessons.title: F with a barre
theory: A barre is the index pressing every string on one fret: lay it on its side, not flat.
F is the E shape barred at fret 1. Move it and you get any major chord.
tips: Don't squeeze harder: pull your arm back and let its weight do the pressing.
tutorials: how to play f barre chord guitar

exercises.title: F four times, all six strings ringing

lessons.title: A minor pentatonic
theory: The pentatonic scale has 5 notes: most rock and blues solos are improvised with it.
Position 1 at fret 5: index on 5, ring or pinky on 7/8.
tutorials: a minor pentatonic scale guitar position 1

exercises.title: Climb the scale, note by note

levels.title: The blues
levels.subtitle: Shuffle, thirds that follow the chords, bends with a target, phrases that answer, and a story in three choruses.

lessons.title: The shuffle and the 12-bar form
theory: Shuffle eighths are long-short, like the first and last notes of a triplet: "daa-da, daa-da".
Hear the form as three turns: bar 5 goes to the IV, bar 9 to the V, bar 11 back home to the I.
Quick change: bar 2 visits the IV and comes back. Both versions are real blues; the recording you play with decides.
The last bar (the V) is the turnaround: it sends you back to the top. To end the song, stay on the I.
tips: Tap your foot on 2 and 4: the backbeat is where the blues feels heavy.
Listen: Freddie King's instrumentals and Muddy Waters' Chicago band are shuffle schools in themselves.

exercises.title: The same line in E, on the low string

lessons.title: Minor third, major third
theory: The minor pentatonic has C over A7, but the chord has C#. The blues lives on that clash: C is the cry, C# the answer.
Every chord has its own pair: C→C# on A7, F→F# on D7, G→G# on E7.
Thirds and sevenths name a chord better than its root: land on one of them right when the chord changes.
In a slow minor blues the minor third is home and doesn't need to resolve (see the minor blues lesson).
tips: Hammer, slide or nudge the minor third up to the major third: don't sit on the minor third over a major chord.
Listening test: play your usual pentatonic, but stop on C#, F# and G# in bars 1, 5 and 9. The changes suddenly appear.
tutorials: blues guitar minor third to major third
mixing major and minor pentatonic blues

exercises.title: Land on each chord's third: C# (A7), F# (D7), G# (E7), C# (A7)

lessons.title: Bends with a target
theory: A bend isn't "push as far as you can": it goes from one note to another, specific note.
Hear the target first: play fret 9 on the G string, then bend fret 7 until it sounds the same.
Hold it: one or two seconds right on pitch, without creeping up or sagging.
Push with two or three fingers together and turn the wrist, as if turning a key.
tips: A half-step bend on the minor third (C → C# over A) is the "curl" that sounds so bluesy.
Stop if you feel sharp pain or numbness; build strength little by little.
Listen: B.B. King and Albert King made a career out of bending to exact notes.

exercises.title: Whole-step bend: G string, fret 7 → E
Whole-step bend: B string, fret 8 → A
Half-step curl: G string, fret 5 → C#

lessons.title: Call and response
theory: The blues talks: one phrase asks, the next one answers. The voice asks and the guitar answers, or your guitar does both.
A phrase has five parts: where it starts, its rhythm, its direction, the note it lands on and how it ends.
A good answer keeps one thing from the question (the rhythm, the direction or the last note) and changes another.
Leave space after each phrase: the silence lets the answer be heard.
tips: Questions end open (on the 5th or the 4th); answers come home (to the root, or to the major third).
Listen: B.B. King's live recordings answer every vocal line with very few notes.
tutorials: call and response blues guitar lesson

exercises.title: The question: it ends open, on E
The answer: it comes home to A

lessons.title: The turnaround
theory: Bars 11 and 12 are the turnaround: a short phrase that leads back to the top of the form.
A chromatic line falling from the 7th to the 5th (G, F#, F, E in A) is the classic way to get there.
It ends on the V chord (E7 in A): it shouldn't sound finished, it should pull you into bar 1.
tips: Play it at the end of every chorus and you'll stop losing the form.
It's the same shape in any key: move it so it starts on the root.

exercises.title: Blues in A at full speed

lessons.title: Slow minor blues: long notes
theory: In a minor blues the minor third (C in A minor) is home: it doesn't need to resolve to the major third.
Fewer notes, more weight: a slow blues exposes the bend, the vibrato and the end of every note.
Delay the vibrato: let the note sound for half a beat, then start it, keeping its center on pitch.
The E7 in bar 9 is the strongest moment: aim at G# there, the only major third in the song.
tips: Mute the string when the phrase ends: the silence keeps the pulse going.
Listen: B.B. King's "The Thrill Is Gone" is a lesson in long notes.

exercises.title: Whole-step bend: high E, fret 8 → D, held 1.5 s
A long answer that lands on C
Slow minor blues in A minor

lessons.title: Eight-bar blues
theory: Not every blues has 12 bars: in the 8-bar form the V arrives as early as bar 2.
I · V · IV · IV · I · V · I-IV · I-V. Don't count it as a short 12-bar: hear its own turns.
Rhythm and lead share the same time: when you go back from a phrase to the chords, the pulse mustn't skip.
tips: Listen: "Key to the Highway" (Big Bill Broonzy, later Derek and the Dominos) is the 8-bar classic.
tutorials: key to the highway guitar lesson rhythm

lessons.title: Three choruses, one story
theory: Chorus 1 states a motif, low and with few notes. Chorus 2 repeats it with a change. Chorus 3 goes higher or louder, then ends clearly.
Develop it by changing one thing at a time: the ending, the register, the rhythm or the dynamics. Change everything and nobody recognizes the motif.
More and faster isn't the only way to build: space, repetition and register build too.
tips: Record the three choruses without stopping. If you make a mistake, keep going: that's practice too.
tutorials: how to build a blues solo three choruses

exercises.title: The same motif, a new ending
Three choruses in A, with an ending

levels.title: Songs
levels.subtitle: Real songs: their chords, their form, the techniques they use, and the chart at your own pace.

lessons.title: November Rain (Guns N' Roses)
theory: The record is tuned a half step down and sounds in B major. In standard tuning you play the same shapes in C: F, Dm, C and G.
The verse walks F → Dm → C: two chords that share notes (F and A) and then a rest on C, the home chord.
The chorus swaps the start: Dm → G → C. G pulls back to C, so every line closes at home.
It's a slow ballad: every chord lasts a full bar. Your job is to change on time and let each one ring.
tips: The F barre is the hard part. If it doesn't ring yet, play the small F (strings 1 to 4) and move to the full barre later.
Change during the last beat of the bar, not after the first beat of the next one.
Strum softly: one long down strum on beat 1, and a light down-down-up at the end of the bar.
Play along with the record only after you retune a half step down; for grading here, stay in standard tuning.

exercises.title: Ring the F barre four times
Ballad bend: G string, fret 7 → E
A slow phrase in C, ending with vibrato
The whole chart at full speed

lessons.title: Comfortably Numb (Pink Floyd)
theory: Standard tuning. The verse is in B minor: Bm → A → G → Em, and back to Bm.
The chorus moves to D major, the relative major of B minor: same notes, a brighter home.
In the chorus, C is borrowed (it isn't in D major): it gives that floating feel before G and A take you back.
The famous solos live in the B minor pentatonic around fret 7 and 10: long bends, wide vibrato and lots of space.
tips: Bm is a barre at fret 2. If it doesn't ring yet, play only strings 1 to 4.
It's slow (about 64 BPM): count four beats per chord out loud before you play along.
In a bend, the target pitch matters more than the speed: go up slowly until it sounds right, then hold it.
Leave silence between phrases. In this style, the space is part of the solo.
tutorials: how to bend in tune guitar

exercises.title: Long bend: B string, fret 10 → B
B minor pentatonic at fret 7, down and up
Bend, release and answer with vibrato
The whole chart at full speed

levels.title: Reading the neck
levels.subtitle: Half steps, intervals by ear and by fret, finding notes and thinking in degrees.

lessons.title: Sharps, flats and half steps
theory: On a piano, going from one key to the very next one (white or black) is a half step. On a guitar, one fret is a half step.
There's a black key between most natural notes. Only E–F and B–C are a half step apart, with nothing in between.
A black key has two names: C♯ (C raised) is the same pitch as D♭ (D lowered). Which name you use depends on the key you're in.
Two frets make a whole step: C to D, E to F♯, B to C♯.
tips: Play a natural note, then the same note one fret higher, and name both ways: F, F♯ = G♭.
tutorials: half steps and whole steps guitar
captions: One octave of a piano: tap a key to hear it. Black keys carry both names.
The natural notes on the 6th and 5th strings. The empty frets between them are the sharps and flats.

exercises.title: Half steps, whole steps and two names
Find the natural notes on the neck
Play the note on the string

lessons.title: Intervals: counting frets
theory: An interval is the distance between two notes, counted in half steps, which on the guitar means frets.
The ones you'll use most: minor 3rd = 3 frets, major 3rd = 4, perfect 4th = 5, perfect 5th = 7, octave = 12.
Across strings the count still works: the next string up starts 5 frets higher (4 between the G and B strings).
Every interval has its own sound: the major 3rd is bright, the minor 3rd darker, the 5th open and hollow.
tips: Hum the two notes after you play them. Linking the sound to the shape is what makes intervals stick.
captions: A major on one string, labeled by degree. The distance from 1 to each number is an interval.

exercises.title: Name the interval by its frets
Play a 3rd, a 5th or an octave
Play a minor 3rd, a 4th or a 6th

lessons.title: Hearing intervals
theory: Ear training links a sound to a name. Start with a few intervals that sound very different, then add the closer ones.
Sing the two notes back after you hear them. If you can sing it, you can find it on the neck.
Naming what you hear and playing it are two different skills, so they're two separate exercises here.
tips: Don't guess fast: replay the pair, sing it, and compare it with intervals you already know.
tutorials: how to recognize intervals by ear

lessons.title: Find the note
theory: Learn the natural notes on the 6th and 5th strings first: they're where the roots of most chord shapes live.
Use the fret markers as landmarks. On the 6th string, frets 3, 5, 7, 9 and 12 are G, A, B, C♯ and E.
The octave shape finds the same note higher up: two strings up and two frets up (three frets when you cross the B string).
tips: Practice in short bursts: five notes, then rest. Accuracy first, speed later.
tutorials: learn the notes on the guitar neck
captions: Natural notes on the 6th and 5th strings.

exercises.title: Mark every one on the low strings

lessons.title: Degrees: a map that moves with the key
theory: A degree names a note by its place in the key: 1 is the root, 3 the third, 5 the fifth. In G the 3rd is B; in A it's C♯.
Degree shapes don't change when the key does: move the root and every degree moves with it.
Learn where 1, 3 and 5 sit around a root. That's every major chord, in every key.
tips: Say degrees, not letters, while you practice a shape: “1, 3, 5” works in any key.
captions: G major around fret 2, labeled by degree. Move it up two frets and it's A major.

levels.title: Reading rhythm II
levels.subtitle: Sixteenths, dotted notes, triplets, syncopation and dictation.

lessons.title: Sixteenth notes
theory: A sixteenth note is a quarter of a beat: four of them fit in every click. It's written with two beams (or two flags). Count "1 e and a" quietly, without speeding up.
tips: Pick down-up-down-up, one stroke per sixteenth. The hand keeps moving even when it doesn't play.

lessons.title: The dotted eighth
theory: A dot next to a note adds half its value. A dotted eighth lasts ¾ of a beat, and it almost always comes with a sixteenth that completes the beat: the limping feel of many riffs.
tips: Think in sixteenths: the dotted eighth lasts three of them, the sixteenth one. "1 – – a 2 – – a".

lessons.title: Triplets
theory: A triplet splits the beat in three equal parts instead of two or four. It's written with a 3 over the group. Count "trip-o-let" or "1-2-3" inside every click.
tips: Lots of blues and 12/8 ballads live on triplets. The shuffle is a triplet with the middle note left out.

lessons.title: Syncopation
theory: Syncopation is when a note starts on a weak spot (on the "and") and holds over the next strong beat. That's the push that makes funk and so much else move forward.
tips: Tap your foot on every beat and play only where it's written. The foot doesn't follow the hand.

theory: In a dictation it goes the other way: the app plays a bar and you choose the notation. It's what happens when you figure out a song by ear.

levels.title: Reading notation
levels.subtitle: From tab to the staff: the treble clef, position by position.

lessons.title: The staff and the clef
theory: The staff has five lines and four spaces: the higher a note sits, the higher it sounds. The clef at the start says which note lives on which line.
Guitar is written in the treble clef, an octave above how it sounds, so its notes fit on the staff. That's why the clef has a small 8 under it.
tips: Notes beyond the staff get ledger lines: short lines that carry the staff up or down.
tutorials: how to read treble clef guitar
captions: The open strings on the staff, from the lowest to the highest.

lessons.title: Open strings on the staff
theory: Start with the open strings: they're the landmarks for everything else. Notice where each one sits, on a line or in a space, and how many ledger lines it needs.
captions: Open strings, from the lowest to the highest.

lessons.title: Natural notes on the low strings
theory: Now the natural notes (no sharps or flats) of the two lowest strings, up to the 5th fret. Each letter of the musical alphabet moves the note one step on the staff, from a line to a space or the other way round.
captions: Naturals on the 6th string: E, F, G, A.
Naturals on the 5th string: A, B, C, D.

lessons.title: Natural notes on every string
theory: With every string, the first position covers more than two octaves. Use the open strings as anchors: find the nearest open string and count steps from it.

exercises.title: Name the note in first position

lessons.title: From the staff to the neck
theory: Reading means knowing where to play. The app shows a note on the staff and you click it on the neck at the exact height: the same note an octave up or down doesn't count.
tips: Some notes exist on two strings (the 5th fret of one string = the next open string). Both count: it's the same pitch.

lessons.title: Sharps and flats on the staff
theory: A sharp (♯) before a note raises it a half step; a flat (♭) lowers it a half step. On the staff the note stays in the same place and just gets the sign in front. On the neck it's the next fret.
captions: F, F♯, G, G♯ on the 6th string.
The same frets spelled with flats: F, G♭, G, A♭.

exercises.title: Name the note, sharps and flats too

lessons.title: Reading in 5th position
theory: Readers don't stay stuck in first position. In 5th position, finger 1 sits on fret 5 and each finger takes care of one fret (5 to 8). The notes on the staff are the same; only where they live on the neck changes.
tips: Use the string above as a shortcut: the 5th fret of one string is the next open string (except G→B, which is the 4th fret).
captions: On the 6th string, frets 5, 7 and 8: A, B, C.

lessons.title: Reading in 7th position
theory: In 7th position (frets 7 to 10), many notes that were open strings in first position become fretted. It's a great position to read scales in sharp keys such as D and A major.
tips: Choose a position before you start reading and stay in it: a still hand makes every note easier to find.

lessons.title: Reading on the guitar
theory: The finish: the note shows up on the staff and you play it on the guitar. It's the first step to reading real notation note by note, the way you read tab.
tips: Play it at the written height: the listener wants that exact note, not the same name an octave away.

exercises.title: Read and play in first position

levels.title: Scales
levels.subtitle: Build scales from their steps, spell them in every key, and play them across the neck.

lessons.title: Building the major scale
theory: The major scale is a pattern of steps: whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half (W W H W W W H).
Start on any note and follow the pattern. From C you get C D E F G A B C, with no sharps or flats.
Each note is a degree, 1 to 7. The half steps always fall between 3–4 and 7–1.
tips: Play it on one string first: you'll see the steps as fret distances (2 2 1 2 2 2 1).
tutorials: how to build the major scale
captions: C major on one string: the frets between neighbors go 2 2 1 2 2 2 1.

lessons.title: The major scale in all 12 keys
theory: A major scale uses each letter from A to G exactly once. So F♯ major has E♯, not F, and G♭ major has C♭, not B.
Keys with sharps go up in fifths: G (1♯), D (2), A (3), E (4), B (5), F♯ (6).
Keys with flats go the other way: F (1♭), B♭ (2), E♭ (3), A♭ (4), D♭ (5), G♭ (6).
The shape on the guitar doesn't care about names: the same fingering works in every key. Spelling matters when you read, write and talk about music.
tips: Write a scale's letters first (one of each), then add the sharps or flats the pattern needs.

lessons.title: Natural minor and the relative minor
theory: The natural minor scale is the major scale started on its 6th degree: A minor has the same notes as C major.
Same notes, different home. A minor sounds sad or serious because everything comes back to A.
From its own root the formula is 1 2 ♭3 4 5 ♭6 ♭7.
Every major key has a relative minor a minor 3rd below its root: G → E minor, F → D minor.
tips: Play C major, then the same notes starting and ending on A. Listen to how the home changes.
captions: A natural minor around fret 5, labeled by degree.

lessons.title: Major scale positions across the neck
theory: One position covers four or five frets, one finger per fret. Five positions connect to cover the whole neck.
Each position starts on a different degree on the 6th string, and the end of one is the start of the next.
Learn them one at a time, saying the root out loud. Then link two neighbors.
tips: Stay in one position for a whole session before you add the next one.
captions: G major, position starting at fret 2.
G major, the next position up (frets 4–8).

exercises.title: Mark the scale in one position
Position at fret 2, up and down

lessons.title: Three notes per string
theory: Three-notes-per-string patterns put exactly three scale notes on each string.
They stretch more, but they make alternate picking even: down-up-down, up-down-up.
Each pattern spans about two octaves and moves diagonally up the neck.
tips: Start slow with strict alternate picking. Speed comes from evenness, not effort.

exercises.title: G major, three notes per string
A minor, three notes per string

lessons.title: Major and minor pentatonic: one shape, two homes
theory: The minor pentatonic has five notes: 1 ♭3 4 5 ♭7. The major pentatonic has 1 2 3 5 6.
A minor pentatonic and C major pentatonic share the same five notes: the box you already know is both.
What changes is the home note. Over A minor aim for A; over C major aim for C.
tips: Play the box over a C chord, then over an Am chord, and end each phrase on its root.
captions: A minor pentatonic at fret 5, by degree.
The same notes as C major pentatonic: only the 1 moved.

lessons.title: Harmonic and melodic minor
theory: Harmonic minor raises the 7th of natural minor: 1 2 ♭3 4 5 ♭6 7. That raised 7th pulls hard toward the root.
It also makes the V chord major: E7 in A minor. That's why it's called harmonic.
Melodic minor raises the 6th as well: 1 2 ♭3 4 5 6 7. Jazz uses it the same way going up and down.
tips: Listen for the jump between ♭6 and 7 in harmonic minor: that gap gives it its exotic sound.
captions: A harmonic minor, by degree.

levels.title: Scale colors
levels.subtitle: Modes, symmetric scales, bebop and altered: the colors of rock and jazz.

lessons.title: Bright modes: Lydian and Mixolydian
theory: A mode uses the major scale's notes with a different home. Compare each mode with the major scale on the same root.
Lydian is major with a ♯4: floating and dreamy.
Mixolydian is major with a ♭7: bluesy, rock, the sound of a dominant chord.
Play a mode over its root held as a drone, and lean on the color note.
tips: Let an open string ring as the drone (G or D) and improvise slowly with the mode on top.
captions: G Mixolydian at fret 2: the b7 is what makes it different from G major.

lessons.title: Dark modes: Dorian, Phrygian and Locrian
theory: Dorian is natural minor with a natural 6: minor, but brighter. You hear it in funk, jazz and a lot of rock solos.
Phrygian is natural minor with a ♭2: dark and tense, with a Spanish flavor.
Locrian has a ♭2 and a ♭5: unstable. Jazz uses it over m7♭5 chords.
tips: Over a minor drone, alternate natural minor and Dorian: the 6th is the only note that changes.
captions: D Dorian, by degree: a minor scale with a natural 6.

lessons.title: Whole-tone and diminished scales
theory: Whole-tone: six notes, all a whole step apart. No note sounds like home, so it floats.
The diminished scales alternate half and whole steps, with eight notes. Half-whole fits dominant 7♭9 chords; whole-half fits diminished chords.
Both are symmetric: the pattern repeats every 2 frets (whole-tone) or every 3 frets (diminished), so one shape moves everywhere.
tips: Learn one fingering, then slide it by its repeat distance and hear that it's the same scale.

lessons.title: Bebop scales
theory: A bebop scale adds one passing tone to a seven-note scale, which makes eight notes.
Dominant bebop adds the natural 7 to Mixolydian. With eight notes, a run of eighth notes that starts on a chord tone on the beat keeps chord tones on the beats.
Major bebop adds a ♭6 to the major scale, for the same reason.
tips: Start the run on the root on beat 1 and descend: listen for the chord tones landing on the beats.

lessons.title: The altered scale
theory: The altered scale is the 7th mode of melodic minor. Over a dominant chord it gives every tension at once: ♭9, ♯9, ♯11 and ♭13.
Over G7 that's G A♭ A♯ B C♯ E♭ F: the root, 3rd and ♭7 stay; the 5th and the 9th are all altered.
Use it on a V7 just before it resolves: maximum tension right before the release.
tips: Resolve every altered phrase to a chord tone of the next chord, a half step away if you can.

levels.title: Building chords
levels.subtitle: Triads, inversions, sus and sixth chords, the seventh family and extensions.

lessons.title: Build a triad
theory: A triad stacks two thirds: root, 3rd and 5th. Major is a major 3rd plus a minor 3rd; minor is a minor 3rd plus a major 3rd.
The 3rd decides major or minor: lower it one fret and C becomes Cm.
Any three strings can hold a triad, as long as you find the three notes.
tips: Before you play a shape, point at its root, 3rd and 5th.
captions: C chord tones up to fret 5, labeled by degree.

exercises.title: Build the triad on the neck

lessons.title: Triad inversions on string sets
theory: An inversion puts a different chord tone in the bass: root position (1 3 5), 1st inversion (3 5 1), 2nd inversion (5 1 3).
On a set of three adjacent strings, the three inversions follow each other up the neck.
Slash names say what's in the bass: C/E is C with E in the bass.
tips: Learn one string set completely before the next: top strings first, then the middle ones.

exercises.title: C on the top three strings

lessons.title: Inversions for smooth bass lines
theory: Inversions let the bass move by step instead of jumping.
C – Em – F – G has a bass that jumps around. C – Em/B – F/A – G makes it walk down: C, B, A, G.
Listen to the bass as its own melody: it ties the chords together.
tips: Play only the bass notes first, then the full chords.
tutorials: slash chords descending bass line guitar

exercises.title: A bass line that walks down

lessons.title: Sus and sixth chords
theory: A sus chord swaps the 3rd for the 2nd (sus2) or the 4th (sus4). With no 3rd it's neither major nor minor: open, waiting.
A sus4 often resolves to the major chord: Dsus4 → D.
A sixth chord adds the 6th to a triad (C6 = C E G A). It's sweet and stable, an alternative to maj7.
tips: Keep the fingers that don't move pressed down when you go from sus to major.

exercises.title: C6 on the top four strings

lessons.title: The seventh-chord family
theory: Put one more third on top of a triad and you get a seventh chord. Five types cover almost all of jazz.
maj7 (1 3 5 7) is lush. 7 (1 3 5 ♭7) is the dominant: it wants to resolve. m7 (1 ♭3 5 ♭7) is mellow.
m7♭5 (1 ♭3 ♭5 ♭7) is the ii chord of a minor key. dim7 (1 ♭3 ♭5 ♭♭7) is symmetric and tense.
m(maj7) (1 ♭3 5 7) is the dark, cinematic one.
tips: Play the same root in all five types and listen to what each change of one note does.

lessons.title: Extensions and altered dominants
theory: Keep stacking thirds past the 7th to get the 9th, the 11th and the 13th: the 2nd, 4th and 6th an octave up.
On a dominant chord the 9th, 11th and 13th can be altered: ♭9, ♯9, ♯11, ♭13. Altered tones add tension before the chord resolves.
On guitar you rarely play every note. Keep the 3rd and the 7th, add the color, and leave out the 5th (and often the root).
tips: Hear each color against the plain 7 chord first: C7, then C9, then C7♯9.

levels.title: CAGED
levels.subtitle: Five chord shapes that fit together and cover the whole neck.

lessons.title: One chord, five places
theory: The open chords C, A, G, E and D all look different. The idea of CAGED is that these five shapes, moved up with a barre, play any major chord in five regions of the neck, each one touching the next.
Going up the neck the order is always C → A → G → E → D, and then it starts again. Knowing which shape you're in tells you where the root, the 3rd and the 5th are, with nothing else to memorize.
tips: Two neighboring shapes share notes where they meet: the edge of one is the start of the next. That's why they cover the neck with no gaps.
tutorials: caged chord shapes up the neck
captions: Every note of C major (1, 3, 5) up to the 15th fret. Each shape is a slice of this map.

lessons.title: The E shape
theory: The E shape is the most used barre: the root sits on the 6th string under finger 1, and the rest of the chord in the next two frets.
captions: C in the E shape, root on the 8th fret.

exercises.title: Find the chord in the E shape
Play G in the E shape, low to high

lessons.title: The A shape
theory: In the A shape the root sits on the 5th string under finger 1. It's the other everyday barre.
captions: C in the A shape, root on the 3rd fret.

exercises.title: Find the chord in the A shape
Play C in the A shape, low to high

lessons.title: The D shape
theory: In the D shape the root sits on the 4th string. The shape is small and lives on the high strings: great for chords up the neck.
captions: C in the D shape, root on the 10th fret.

exercises.title: Find the chord in the D shape

lessons.title: The C shape
theory: In the C shape the root is on the 5th string again, but under finger 3 or 4: the chord reaches back toward the nut.
captions: D in the C shape, root on the 5th fret.

exercises.title: Find the chord in the C shape

lessons.title: The G shape
theory: The G shape also reaches back, with the root on the 6th string under finger 3 or 4. It's the widest of the five, and many players use only part of it.
captions: C in the G shape, root on the 8th fret.

exercises.title: Find the chord in the G shape

lessons.title: Connecting the five shapes
theory: Now all of them together. The app picks the chord and the shape; you find 1, 3 and 5 in that position. Before you click, remember the order C → A → G → E → D and where each shape keeps its root.
captions: G major over the whole neck: try to see the five shapes, one after another.

exercises.title: The five shapes of G, up the neck

lessons.title: Minor shapes
theory: The E, A and D shapes also come in minor: just lower the 3rd a half step. With them you can play any minor chord in three regions.
captions: Am in the Em shape, root on the 5th fret.

exercises.title: Find the minor chord in the Em, Am or Dm shape
Play Am in the Em and Am shapes

levels.title: Harmony
levels.subtitle: The chords that live in a key, written as roman numerals, in major and minor.

lessons.title: The chords of a key
theory: Build a triad on each degree of the major scale, using only notes of the scale: you get I ii iii IV V vi vii°.
Uppercase numerals are major, lowercase are minor, and ° is diminished. The pattern is the same in every key.
In C: C Dm Em F G Am B°. In G: G Am Bm C D Em F♯°.
Numerals let you move a song to any key in your head: I–V–vi–IV is the same progression everywhere.
tips: Say the numeral while you play each chord of a song you know.

exercises.title: Every chord of C, on the top strings

lessons.title: Sevenths and ninths in a key
theory: Stack one more third and every degree gets a seventh chord: Imaj7 ii7 iii7 IVmaj7 V7 vi7 viiø7.
A major key has only one dominant 7: the V7. It's the chord that pulls you home.
Add the 9th where the scale allows it: Imaj9, ii9, IVmaj9, V9 and vi9 work. On iii and vii the 9th would be ♭9, so they usually stay sevenths.
tips: Play the seven chords in order, then just ii–V–I: hear how much the V7 wants to go home.
tutorials: harmonizing the major scale in sevenths

lessons.title: Seventh chords in minor keys
theory: Natural minor gives you i7, iiø7, IIImaj7, iv7, v7, VImaj7 and VII7. Its v chord is minor (Em7 in A minor), so it doesn't pull home strongly.
Harmonic minor raises the 7th, and now the V is a dominant 7 (E7 in A minor) that pulls hard to i.
Most minor-key songs mix both: natural minor for color, and the V7 from harmonic minor for the cadence.
tips: Play Am – Em – Am, then Am – E7 – Am, and compare how the ending feels.

levels.title: Harmonic function
levels.subtitle: What each chord does, by name and by ear: cadences, secondary dominants, borrowed chords.

lessons.title: Tonic, subdominant, dominant
theory: Every chord of the key has a job. The tonic (I, and also iii and vi) is home: rest. The subdominant (IV and ii) moves away from home. The dominant (V and vii°) builds tension and asks to go back to the tonic.
Chords that share notes tend to share their job: C, Em and Am all have E in them; F and Dm share F and A; G7 and B° share B, D and F.
tips: Almost every song tells this story in cycles: it leaves the tonic, passes the subdominant, reaches the dominant and comes back.

lessons.title: By ear: I, IV and V
theory: I, IV and V are the major chords of the key and they hold up thousands of songs. The app plays the tonic and then another chord: you say which degree it is.
tips: The IV sounds like opening a door; the V sounds like something is missing. Sing the tonic over it: on the V it feels uncomfortable.

lessons.title: By ear: ii and vi join in
theory: Now the minor chords of the key join in: ii (subdominant) and vi (the relative tonic). The vi sounds like the sad side of home; the ii like a softer IV.

exercises.title: I, ii, IV, V or vi?

lessons.title: By ear in a minor key
theory: In a minor key the major chords VI and VII give that epic sound of so much rock and metal. The app plays the i and then another chord of the minor key.
tips: In practice many minor songs swap the minor v for a major V, borrowed from harmonic minor, for a stronger pull home.

lessons.title: Progressions everybody uses
theory: Some sequences of degrees show up in so many songs that they became clichés: I–V–vi–IV (all of pop), I–IV–V–I (rock and blues), ii–V–I (jazz and bossa) and, in minor, i–VI–III–VII (epic rock).
Thinking in degrees is what lets you play the same song in any key, or spot the progression of a new song in seconds.

lessons.title: Cadences
theory: A cadence is how a phrase ends. Authentic: V → I, the strongest ending. Plagal: IV → I, the softer "amen". Half cadence: the phrase stops on V, like a comma asking for more. Deceptive: V → vi, the ear expected I and got something else.
Think of the last chord's job: ending on I is conclusive (authentic or plagal); ending on V is suspended (half); a V that goes elsewhere is deceptive.
tutorials: cadences explained authentic plagal half deceptive

lessons.title: Secondary dominants
theory: Any chord of the key (except vii°) can get its own dominant: the seventh chord a fifth above it. In C major, A7 is the V7 of Dm (written V7/ii); E7 is the V7 of Am (V7/vi); D7 is the V7 of G (V7/V).
That chord brings one note from outside the key, a half step under the chord it wants to reach: E7 brings G♯, which leads up to A.
tips: See a 7 chord that isn't the V of the key? Look a 4th above it (or a 5th below): that's where it wants to go.

lessons.title: Borrowed chords
theory: A major key can borrow chords from the minor key with the same tonic. In C major the usual ones are Fm (iv), B♭ (♭VII), A♭ (♭VI) and E♭ (♭III). The minor iv gives that nostalgic squeeze (F → Fm → C); the ♭VII, a rock flavor.
tips: See a chord with a flat in a sharp key (or a minor chord on IV)? Think of a loan from the parallel minor.

levels.title: Voicings
levels.subtitle: Shells, drop-2, drop-3, voice leading and guide tones: chords the way jazz guitarists play them.

lessons.title: Shell voicings
theory: A shell has three notes: root, 3rd and 7th. That's enough to say exactly what the chord is.
Two shapes cover everything: root on the 6th string (1–7–3) and root on the 5th string (1–3–7).
Alternating them keeps your hand in one place: Dm7 (root on the 5th) → G7 (root on the 6th) → Cmaj7 (root on the 5th).
tips: Mute the strings you don't use with the side of your fingers: shells should sound like three clean notes.

exercises.title: Which notes are the guide tones?

lessons.title: Drop-2 voicings
theory: Start with a close four-note chord and drop the second voice from the top down an octave: that's drop 2.
It spreads the chord so it fits on four adjacent strings: the top four (1–4) or the middle four (2–5).
Every chord has four drop-2 inversions on each string set, one for each chord tone in the bass.
tips: Learn one chord's four inversions on one string set, then move the same idea to other chord types.

exercises.title: Cmaj7 on the top four strings

lessons.title: Drop-3 voicings
theory: Drop the third voice from the top instead and you get drop 3: a wider sound, with the bass on the 6th or 5th string and one string skipped.
Drop-3 shapes are the classic big-band comping chords: a bass note, then three notes on the middle strings.
tips: Mute the skipped string with the finger that plays the bass.

lessons.title: Voice leading
theory: Voice leading means moving each note of a chord to the nearest note of the next chord.
Common tones stay put and the rest move by a half or a whole step. The progression sounds smooth even when the chords change a lot.
Choose the next inversion by its top note (the melody) or by its bass, and let the other voices find the closest notes.
Try it in the chord finder: write a progression and it chooses the voicings for you.
tips: Hold the notes that repeat between two chords: if a finger doesn't need to move, don't move it.

lessons.title: Guide-tone lines
theory: A chord's guide tones are its 3rd and 7th: they tell major from minor, and dominant from major 7th.
Through a ii–V–I they move by a half step or not at all: the 7th of one chord falls to the 3rd of the next.
Play just those two notes per chord, then a single line through them. It's the skeleton of a jazz solo.
tips: Sing the guide-tone line while a friend (or the app) plays the chords.

levels.title: Jazz foundations
levels.subtitle: ii–V–I in every key, minor ii–V–i, turnarounds, tritone subs, the jazz blues, song form and comping.

lessons.title: The major ii–V–I
theory: ii–V–I is the most common move in jazz: a minor 7 on the 2nd degree, a dominant 7 on the 5th, and home on the major 7.
In C that's Dm7 – G7 – Cmaj7. The bass goes up a 4th each time, and the guide tones fall by a half step.
Jazz moves through keys all the time, so the goal is to play it in all twelve without thinking.
tips: Learn it in C and F first, then add one key a day. The three charts cover all twelve.
tutorials: ii V I jazz guitar beginner
ii V I in all 12 keys guitar

lessons.title: The minor ii–V–i
theory: In a minor key the ii is half-diminished (m7♭5), the V is a dominant with a ♭9 and the i is minor: Bm7♭5 – E7♭9 – Am6 in A minor.
The ♭9 of E7 is F, a note of A minor: that's what makes the V sound like it belongs to the minor key.
On the i, m6 is the classic jazz choice; m(maj7) and m7 work too.
tips: Listen for the F in E7♭9 falling to E: it's the sound of the minor ii–V–i.
tutorials: minor ii V i jazz guitar

lessons.title: Turnarounds
theory: A turnaround is a short loop that brings you back to the top: two bars that lead to the I.
I–vi–ii–V is the basic one. iii–VI–ii–V starts away from home and makes the VI dominant (A7 in C) to pull toward ii.
Each chord can be replaced by one that shares its job: that's how one turnaround becomes many.
tips: Loop each turnaround for a minute before you move on: they're meant to be repeated.
tutorials: I vi ii V turnaround guitar

lessons.title: Tritone substitution
theory: G7 and D♭7 share their guide tones: G7 has B and F, D♭7 has F and C♭ (the same pitch as B).
So D♭7 can stand in for G7: Dm7 – D♭7 – Cmaj7. The bass now slides down by half steps.
Any dominant can be replaced by the one a tritone (6 frets) away.
tips: Play the guide tones of G7, then of D♭7: the same two frets, a different bass under them.

lessons.title: Jazz blues in F
theory: The jazz blues keeps the 12-bar form of the blues and adds ii–V moves that point at the next chord.
Bar 4 is a ii–V into B♭7, bar 8 is D7 (a secondary dominant) setting up Gm7, and bars 11–12 turn around to the top.
Every chord is a dominant or part of a ii–V, so the shell shapes you know cover the whole tune.
tips: Play it once with shells only, then once with the etude in the last lesson of the next level.
tutorials: jazz blues in F guitar chords

exercises.title: The whole form at full speed

lessons.title: The 32-bar song form
theory: Many jazz tunes have 32 bars in four sections of eight: A A B A. The A is the main idea and the B (the bridge) is the contrast.
Our A uses I–vi–ii–V loops; our bridge moves to the IV chord and works its way back with ii–Vs.
Knowing the form is how you keep your place: count bars in groups of eight, and feel where the bridge begins.
tips: Before you play, say the form out loud: “A, A, bridge, A.”

lessons.title: Comping rhythms
theory: Comping is accompanying: chords played in rhythm behind a melody or a solo.
Four to the bar is steady and even. The Charleston figure hits beat 1 and the “and” of 2.
An anticipation plays the next chord an eighth early, on the “and” of 4, which pushes the music forward.
Space is part of comping too: one held chord per bar leaves room for the soloist.
tips: Keep the chords short (lift the pressure right after the strum) so the rhythm is clear.

levels.title: Jazz language
levels.subtitle: Swing, walking bass, arpeggios, approach notes, enclosures, eighth-note lines and etudes.

lessons.title: Swing feel
theory: Swing plays pairs of eighth notes long–short instead of even: the second one of each pair lands late.
Light swing puts it at about 60% of the beat; hard swing at about two thirds, like a triplet with the first two notes tied.
In this app a chart can be straight, light or hard: playback swings the offbeats, and the listener allows a wider timing window.
tips: Turn on swung eighths in the metronome (Tools) and say “doo-ba doo-ba” along with it.
tutorials: how to swing eighth notes guitar

exercises.title: Light swing, four to the bar

lessons.title: Walking bass on guitar
theory: A walking bass plays one note per beat. Beat 1 is the root of the chord, so everyone hears the harmony.
Beats 2 and 3 are chord tones (or scale notes) that move away from the root.
Beat 4 is an approach: a half step below or above the next root, so the line walks into it.
tips: Play with your thumb or a light pick stroke, and let each note last its full beat.
tutorials: walking bass on guitar for beginners

exercises.title: Walk the first bars of the F blues

lessons.title: Arpeggios over the changes
theory: Playing the arpeggio of each chord as it goes by is the clearest way to make a line follow the harmony.
Stay in one position and start each new arpeggio on the chord tone closest to where you are.
Four notes per chord, one per beat: the changes become audible even with no one comping.
tips: Say the chord name at each change. If you lose your place, stop on a root and start again.
tutorials: playing through ii V I arpeggios

lessons.title: Approach notes
theory: An approach note leads into a chord tone from one step away: a half step below (chromatic) or the scale note above (diatonic).
Put the approach on the offbeat and the chord tone on the beat: the target sounds strong and the line sounds intentional.
Aim for 3rds and 7ths: they're the notes that say which chord it is.
tips: Exaggerate the target: play it a little louder than the approach.

lessons.title: Enclosures
theory: An enclosure surrounds the target: the scale note above, the half step below, then the target.
It delays the chord tone by two notes, which builds a little tension before it lands.
Enclose the 3rd of each chord first, then the 7th, then the root.
tips: Practice one enclosure on one chord until it's automatic, then link the chords.

lessons.title: Eighth-note lines from a chord tone
theory: Start on a chord tone on beat 1 and run eight notes of the chord's scale: Dorian over m7, Mixolydian over 7, major over maj7.
Starting on the 3rd or the 7th makes the line sound like the chord right away.
When a run would leave the position, turn around: the line changes direction but keeps going.
tips: Start at 60 BPM with swung eighths. Evenness first, then speed.
tutorials: how to play through changes with scales

lessons.title: Three short etudes
theory: An etude is a short piece that puts several ideas together. These three were written for this course.
“Small steps” walks through a ii–V–I with arpeggio shapes and a 7th that falls to the next 3rd.
“Minor turn” uses the ♭9 of the V chord in a minor ii–V–i, and “Blue F” mixes chord tones with the blue note over the F blues.
tips: Learn each etude by ear and by tab, then play it over its chart.

lessons.title: Ear stretch: tone rows
theory: A tone row uses all twelve notes once each, in any order. No note is home, so you can't lean on a key.
Reading and playing rows stretches your ear and your knowledge of the neck at the same time.
This one is optional: a challenge for when the rest of the level feels easy.
tips: Sing each note before you play it. If you can't sing it, play it and sing it back.

exercises.title: A row in the low frets
